args.content: import os import numpy as np import pandas as pd os.environ["YDATA_SUPPRESS_BANNER"] = "1" from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport, compare from ydata_profiling.config import Settings results = [] def check(name, fn): try: fn() results.append((name, "OK")) except Exception as e: results.append((name, f"FAIL: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")) # 1. unique/distinct stats def t1(): df = pd.DataFrame({"values": [1, 2, 2, None]}) p = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False) v = p.get_description().variables["values"] assert v["is_unique"] is False or v["is_unique"] == False assert v["n_distinct"] == 2 assert abs(v["p_distinct"] - 2 / 3) < 1e-6 check("univariate unique", t1) # 2. correlations def t2(): df = pd.DataFrame({ "num1": np.random.rand(100), "num2": np.random.rand(100), "cat": np.random.choice(["A", "B"], 100), }) p = ProfileReport(df, correlations={"pearson": {"calculate": True}, "spearman": {"calculate": True}}, progress_bar=False) html = p.to_html() assert "Pearson" in html or "pearson" in html desc = p.get_description() assert "pearson" in desc.correlations check("correlations", t2) # 3. duplicates def t3(): from ydata_profiling.model.duplicates import get_duplicates df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 2, 1], "b": [3, 4, 4, 3]}) config = Settings() metrics, dups = get_duplicates(config, df, list(df.columns)) assert metrics["n_duplicates"] == 2 assert metrics["p_duplicates"] == 0.5 check("duplicates", t3) # 4. time series def t4(): dates = pd.date_range(start="2023-01-01", periods=100, freq="D") df = pd.DataFrame({"date": dates, "value": np.sin(np.arange(100))}) p = ProfileReport(df, tsmode=True, sortby="date", progress_bar=False) html = p.to_html() assert len(html) > 1000 check("timeseries", t4) # 5. export formats def t5(): df = pd.DataFrame({"a": range(10), "b": range(10)}) p = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True, html={"inline": False, "style": {"theme": "united"}}, progress_bar=False) p.to_file("/tmp/smoke_report.html") assert os.path.exists("/tmp/smoke_report.html") check("export", t5) # 6. custom sample def t6(): df = pd.DataFrame({"test": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]}) mock = pd.DataFrame({"make": ["A", "B"], "price": [100, 200]}) p = ProfileReport(df, sample={"name": "Mock", "data": mock, "caption": "Synthetic sample"}, minimal=True, progress_bar=False) s = p.get_description().sample[0] assert s.name == "Mock" assert s.caption == "Synthetic sample" check("custom sample", t6) # 7. sensitive mode def t7(): df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Alice", "Bob"]}) p = ProfileReport(df, sensitive=True, progress_bar=False) html = p.to_html() assert "Alice" not in html and "Bob" not in html check("sensitive", t7) # 8. interactions def t8(): df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(10, 5), columns=[f"col{i}" for i in range(5)]) p = ProfileReport(df, interactions={"continuous": True, "targets": ["col0", "col1"]}, progress_bar=False) desc = p.get_description() assert len(desc.scatter) > 0 check("interactions", t8) # 9. compare def t9(): df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": range(10)}) df2 = pd.DataFrame({"a": range(10, 20)}) p1 = ProfileReport(df1, title="Dataset 1", progress_bar=False) p2 = ProfileReport(df2, title="Dataset 2", progress_bar=False) c = compare([p1, p2]) html = c.to_html() assert len(html) > 1000 check("compare", t9) # 10. env var override def t10(): os.environ["PROFILE_TITLE"] = "Testing Title" try: r = ProfileReport(pool_size=3) assert r.config.title == "Testing Title" r.config.pool_size = 1 assert r.config.pool_size == 1 finally: del os.environ["PROFILE_TITLE"] check("env override", t10) # 11. formatters def t11(): from ydata_profiling.report.formatters import fmt_numeric, fmt_bytesize, fmt_color assert fmt_numeric(1e8, 3) == "1 × 108", fmt_numeric(1e8, 3) assert fmt_bytesize(1024) == "1.0 KiB" assert fmt_color("Warning", "red") == 'Warning' check("formatters", t11) # 13. index name conflicts def t13(): df = pd.DataFrame({"foo": [1, 2, 3]}, index=pd.Index([1, 2, 3], name="foo")) p = ProfileReport(df, progress_bar=False) html = p.to_html() assert len(html) > 1000 check("index conflict", t13) # 15. cat freq plot config def t15(): df = pd.DataFrame({"cat": ["A"] * 5 + ["B"] * 5}) p = ProfileReport(df, progress_bar=False) p.config.plot.cat_freq.type = "pie" p.config.plot.cat_freq.colors = ["gold", "blue"] p.invalidate_cache("rendering") html = p.to_html() assert len(html) > 1000 check("cat freq pie", t15) # 16. HTML component def t16(): from ydata_profiling.report.presentation.flavours.html.frequency_table import HTMLFrequencyTable item = HTMLFrequencyTable(rows=[{"count": 10, "percentage": 1.0, "label": "Pizza", "width": 1.0}], redact=False) html = item.render() assert "Pizza" in html check("html component", t16) # 18. empty df raises; all-missing works def t18(): try: ProfileReport(pd.DataFrame(), progress_bar=False) raise AssertionError("should have raised") except ValueError: pass df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [None, None, None], "b": [None, None, None]}) p = ProfileReport(df, title="Data with Missing Values", progress_bar=False) html = p.to_html() assert len(html) > 1000 check("boundaries", t18) # 19. type_schema + dataframe decorator def t19(): import ydata_profiling # noqa df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}) p = df.profile_report(minimal=True, progress_bar=False) assert p.get_description().table["n"] == 3 check("df decorator", t19) # 20. dump/load def t20(): df = pd.DataFrame({"a": range(10)}) p = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False) p.to_html() data = p.dumps() p2 = ProfileReport() p2.loads(data) assert p2.to_html() is not None check("serialize", t20) for name, status in results: print(f"{status:8s} {name}")

"""Logic for alerting the user on possibly problematic patterns in the data (e.g. high number of zeros , constant
values, high correlations)."""

from enum import Enum, auto, unique
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Set

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ydata_profiling.config import Settings
from ydata_profiling.model.correlations import perform_check_correlation
from ydata_profiling.utils.styles import get_alert_styles


def fmt_percent(value: float, edge_cases: bool = True) -> str:
    """Format a ratio as a percentage.

    Args:
        edge_cases: Check for edge cases?
        value: The ratio.

    Returns:
        The percentage with 1 point precision.
    """
    if edge_cases and round(value, 3) == 0 and value > 0:
        return "< 0.1%"
    if edge_cases and round(value, 3) == 1 and value < 1:
        return "> 99.9%"

    return f"{value*100:2.1f}%"


@unique
class AlertType(Enum):
    """Alert types"""

    CONSTANT = auto()
    """This variable has a constant value."""

    ZEROS = auto()
    """This variable contains zeros."""

    HIGH_CORRELATION = auto()
    """This variable is highly correlated."""

    HIGH_CARDINALITY = auto()
    """This variable has a high cardinality."""

    UNSUPPORTED = auto()
    """This variable is unsupported."""

    DUPLICATES = auto()
    """This variable contains duplicates."""

    NEAR_DUPLICATES = auto()
    """This variable contains duplicates."""

    SKEWED = auto()
    """This variable is highly skewed."""

    IMBALANCE = auto()
    """This variable is imbalanced."""

    MISSING = auto()
    """This variable contains missing values."""

    INFINITE = auto()
    """This variable contains infinite values."""

    TYPE_DATE = auto()
    """This variable is likely a datetime, but treated as categorical."""

    UNIQUE = auto()
    """This variable has unique values."""

    DIRTY_CATEGORY = auto()
    """This variable is a categories with potential fuzzy values, and for that reason might incur in consistency issues."""

    CONSTANT_LENGTH = auto()
    """This variable has a constant length."""

# Contributing to ydata-profiling

Thank you for your interest in contributing to ydata-profiling! This guide
summarizes how to get involved. For a more detailed walkthrough, see the
[contribution guidelines](docs/support-contribution/contribution_guidelines.md)
in the documentation.

## Ways to contribute

- **Report bugs**: open an issue using the bug report form. Include a minimal
  reproducible example, the ydata-profiling version, and the full traceback.
- **Request features**: open an issue using the feature request form and
  describe the use case you are trying to solve.
- **Improve documentation**: fix typos, clarify sections, or add examples.
- **Submit code**: bug fixes, new features, and performance improvements are
  all welcome via pull requests.

## Development setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling.git
cd ydata-profiling
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
make install-dev
```

This installs the package in editable mode with the test, notebook, and
linting dependencies, and sets up the pre-commit hooks (black, isort, and
standard checks).

## Workflow

1. Fork the repository and create a branch from `develop`.
2. Make your changes. Add tests for new behavior and update documentation
   when relevant.
3. Run `make lint` and `make test` and make sure both pass.
4. Commit using [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
   (e.g. `fix: handle empty categorical columns`), enforced by commitlint.
5. Open a pull request against `develop` and fill in the PR template.

## Code style

- Code is formatted with [black](https://github.com/psf/black) and imports are
  sorted with [isort](https://pycqa.github.io/isort/). The pre-commit hooks
  run both automatically.
- Keep changes minimal and focused; large refactors should be discussed in an
  issue first.

## Reporting security issues

Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.
Contact the maintainers at opensource@ydata.ai instead.

name: Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [master, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [master, develop]

concurrency:
  group: tests-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  pytest:
    name: Python ${{ matrix.python-version }} on ${{ matrix.os }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest]
        python-version: ["3.9", "3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: pip

      - name: Upgrade packaging tools
        run: python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel

      - name: Install package with test dependencies
        run: python -m pip install -e ".[test,unicode]"

      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          python -m pytest tests/ \
            --cov=ydata_profiling \
            --cov-report=xml \
            -v

      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        if: matrix.python-version == '3.11' && matrix.os == 'ubuntu-latest'
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          file: ./coverage.xml
          fail_ci_if_error: false

name: Bug Report
description: File a bug report to help us improve ydata-profiling
title: "Bug Report: "
labels: ["bug", "triage"]
body:
  - type: markdown
    attributes:
      value: |
        Thanks for taking the time to fill out this bug report!
        Please search existing issues before submitting a new one.

  - type: textarea
    id: current-behaviour
    attributes:
      label: Current Behaviour
      description: A clear and concise description of what the bug is, including the full error message and traceback if applicable.
      placeholder: Tell us what happened.
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: textarea
    id: expected-behaviour
    attributes:
      label: Expected Behaviour
      description: A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen.
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: textarea
    id: data-description
    attributes:
      label: Data Description
      description: |
        Describe the data that triggers the issue: column types, size, missing values, etc.
        If possible, provide code that generates synthetic data reproducing the issue —
        please do not share confidential data.
    validations:
      required: false

  - type: textarea
    id: reproducible-code
    attributes:
      label: Code that reproduces the bug
      description: A minimal, self-contained code snippet that reproduces the problem.
      render: Python
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: input
    id: pandas-profiling-version
    attributes:
      label: pandas-profiling/ydata-profiling version
      description: Output of `pip show ydata-profiling` or `ydata_profiling.__version__`.
      placeholder: v4.16.1
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: dropdown
    id: os
    attributes:
      label: Operating System
      options:

"""Tests for the basic ProfileReport workflow."""
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport


class TestBasicUsage:
    def test_mixed_types_report(self, mixed_df):
        report = ProfileReport(mixed_df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        desc = report.get_description()
        assert desc.table["n"] == 50
        assert desc.table["n_vars"] == 5
        assert set(desc.variables.keys()) == {
            "numeric",
            "categorical",
            "boolean",
            "datetime",
            "text",
        }

    def test_variable_types_detected(self, mixed_df):
        report = ProfileReport(mixed_df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        types = {k: str(v["type"]) for k, v in report.get_description().variables.items()}
        assert types["numeric"] == "Numeric"
        assert types["categorical"] == "Categorical"
        assert types["boolean"] == "Boolean"
        assert types["datetime"] == "DateTime"
        assert types["text"] == "Text"

    def test_minimal_mode(self, small_df):
        report = ProfileReport(small_df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        desc = report.get_description()
        assert desc.table["n"] == 10
        # minimal mode disables expensive analyses
        assert report.config.interactions.continuous is False
        assert report.config.correlations["pearson"].calculate is False
        assert report.config.missing_diagrams["bar"] is False

    def test_title_and_html_render(self, small_df):
        report = ProfileReport(
            small_df, title="My Test Report", minimal=True, progress_bar=False
        )
        html = report.to_html()
        assert "My Test Report" in html
        assert len(html) > 1000

    def test_all_missing_column(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [None, None, None], "b": [1, 2, 3]})
        report = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        desc = report.get_description()
        assert desc.table["n_cells_missing"] == 3


class TestExports:
    def test_to_json(self, small_df):
        report = ProfileReport(small_df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        data = json.loads(report.to_json())
        assert "table" in data
        assert "variables" in data
        assert data["table"]["n"] == 10

    def test_to_file_html_and_json(self, small_df, tmp_path):
        report = ProfileReport(small_df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        html_path = tmp_path / "report.html"
        json_path = tmp_path / "report.json"
        report.to_file(html_path)
        report.to_file(json_path)
        assert html_path.exists() and html_path.stat().st_size > 1000
        assert json_path.exists()
        parsed = json.loads(json_path.read_text())
        assert parsed["table"]["n"] == 10

    def test_to_file_unsupported_extension(self, small_df, tmp_path):
        report = ProfileReport(small_df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            report.to_file(tmp_path / "report.csv")

    def test_dumps_loads_roundtrip(self, small_df):
        report = ProfileReport(small_df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        report.to_html()  # trigger rendering so the cache is serialized
        data = report.dumps()
        assert isinstance(data, bytes)

        loaded = ProfileReport()
        loaded.loads(data)
        assert loaded.to_html() is not None
        assert loaded.get_description().table["n"] == 10


class TestModes:
    def test_tsmode(self):
        dates = pd.date_range(start="2023-01-01", periods=50, freq="D")
        df = pd.DataFrame({"date": dates, "value": np.sin(np.arange(50))})
        report = ProfileReport(df, tsmode=True, sortby="date", progress_bar=False)
        assert report.config.vars.timeseries.active is True
        html = report.to_html()
        assert len(html) > 1000

    def test_sensitive_mode_redacts_values(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]})
        report = ProfileReport(df, sensitive=True, progress_bar=False)
        html = report.to_html()
        assert "Alice" not in html
        assert "Bob" not in html
        assert "Carol" not in html

    def test_empty_dataframe_raises(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            ProfileReport(pd.DataFrame(), progress_bar=False)

    def test_dataframe_decorator(self, small_df):
        import ydata_profiling  # noqa: F401  (registers df.profile_report)

        report = small_df.profile_report(minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
        assert isinstance(report, ProfileReport)
        assert report.get_description().table["n"] == 10

    def test_index_name_conflict(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"foo": [1, 2, 3]}, index=pd.Index([1, 2, 3], name="foo"))
        report = ProfileReport(df, progress_bar=False)
        assert len(report.to_html()) > 1000

"""Tests for get_description() output structure and statistics."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def report():
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "num1": np.linspace(0, 1, 50),
            "num2": np.linspace(0, 1, 50) ** 2,
            "cat": np.tile(["A", "B"], 25),
        }
    )
    return ProfileReport(
        df,
        correlations={"pearson": {"calculate": True}},
        progress_bar=False,
    )


class TestDescriptionStructure:
    def test_top_level_keys(self, report):
        desc = report.get_description().dict()
        for key in [
            "analysis",
            "table",
            "variables",
            "scatter",
            "correlations",
            "missing",
            "alerts",
            "package",
            "sample",
        ]:
            assert key in desc, key

    def test_table_stats(self, report):
        table = report.get_description().table
        assert table["n"] == 50
        assert table["n_vars"] == 3
        assert table["n_cells_missing"] == 0
        assert table["n_duplicates"] == 0
        assert table["memory_size"] > 0

    def test_variables_stats(self, report):
        variables = report.get_description().variables
        assert set(variables.keys()) == {"num1", "num2", "cat"}
        num1 = variables["num1"]
        assert num1["count"] == 50
        assert num1["n_missing"] == 0
        assert abs(num1["mean"] - 0.5) < 1e-9
        assert num1["min"] == 0.0
        assert num1["max"] == 1.0

    def test_correlations_present_when_enabled(self, report):
        correlations = report.get_description().correlations
        assert "pearson" in correlations
        pearson = correlations["pearson"]
        assert pearson.loc["num1", "num1"] == pytest.approx(1.0)

    def test_sample_present(self, report):
        sample = report.get_description().sample
        assert len(sample) > 0
        assert sample[0].name == "First rows"


class TestUnivariateStats:
    def test_unique_and_distinct(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"values": [1, 2, 2, None]})
        desc = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False).get_description()
        v = desc.variables["values"]
        assert not v["is_unique"]
        assert v["n_distinct"] == 2
        assert v["p_distinct"] == pytest.approx(2 / 3)
        assert v["n_missing"] == 1
        assert v["count"] == 3

    def test_all_unique_column(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"values": range(10)})
        desc = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False).get_description()
        v = desc.variables["values"]
        assert v["is_unique"]
        assert v["n_unique"] == 10

    def test_monotonic_stats(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"up": range(10), "down": range(10, 0, -1)})
        desc = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True, progress_bar=False).get_description()
        assert desc.variables["up"]["monotonic_increase"]
        assert desc.variables["down"]["monotonic_decrease"]

    def test_custom_sample(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"test": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]})
        mock = pd.DataFrame({"make": ["A", "B"], "price": [100, 200]})
        report = ProfileReport(
            df,
            sample={"name": "Mock", "data": mock, "caption": "Synthetic sample"},
            minimal=True,
            progress_bar=False,
        )
        sample = report.get_description().sample[0]
        assert sample.name == "Mock"
        assert sample.caption == "Synthetic sample"
        assert len(sample.data) == 2

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def report():
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "num1": np.linspace(0, 1, 50),
            "num2": np.linspace(0, 1, 50) ** 2,
            "cat": np.tile(["A", "B"], 25),

    return ProfileReport(
        df,
        correlations={"pearson": {"calculate": True}},

class TestDescriptionStructure:
    def test_top_level_keys(self, report):
        desc = report.get_description().dict()
        for key in [
            "analysis",
            "table",
            "variables",
            "scatter",
            "correlations",
            "missing",
            "alerts",
            "package",
            "sample",
        ]:
            assert key in desc, key

    def test_table_stats(self, report):
        table = report.get_description().table
        assert table["n"] == 50
        assert table["n_vars"] == 3
        assert table["n_cells_missing"] == 0
        assert table["n_duplicates"] == 0

    def test_variables_stats(self, report):

# ydata-profiling

**One line of code. A complete picture of your data.**

`ydata-profiling` generates rich, interactive profile reports from pandas
(and Spark) DataFrames. For each column it computes the inferred type,
descriptive statistics, the most frequent values, and a histogram, and for
the dataset as a whole it surfaces missing values, duplicate rows, and
correlations between variables.

```python
import pandas as pd
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

df = pd.read_csv("my_data.csv")
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="My data report")
profile.to_file("report.html")
```

The resulting HTML report is self-contained and can be shared with anyone,
embedded in notebooks, or exported as JSON for programmatic consumption.

## Why profiling?

Exploratory data analysis is the first step of every data science workflow,
and also the most repetitive. Writing the same `df.describe()`, null counts,
and distribution plots for every new dataset is slow and error-prone.
ydata-profiling automates this boilerplate so you can spend your time
interpreting the data instead of summarizing it, and it catches data quality
issues — high cardinality, skewness, constant columns, unexpected
correlations — that ad-hoc inspection routinely misses.

## Where to next?

- New here? Start with the [installation guide](getting-started/installation.md)
  and the [quickstart](getting-started/quickstart.md).
- Working with large or time series data? See the
  [features](features/big_data.md) section.
- Want to tune the report? Read about the
  [advanced settings](advanced_settings/available_settings.md).
- Something not working? Check the
  [common issues](support-contribution/common_issues.md) page.

# Overview

ydata-profiling is the successor of `pandas-profiling`, the widely used
library for exploratory data analysis of pandas DataFrames. It extends the
original project with support for time series datasets, dataset comparison,
Spark DataFrames, and an improved report design, while keeping the familiar
one-line API.

## Key capabilities

- **Type inference**: columns are automatically detected as numeric,
  categorical, boolean, date, text, URL, file path, or image, and each type
  gets statistics appropriate to it.
- **Data quality alerts**: the report flags constant and duplicated columns,
  high cardinality, heavy skewness, missing values, and more.
- **Correlations**: Spearman, Pearson, Kendall, Cramér's V, and Phik (φk)
  correlation matrices, with automatic selection available.
- **Dataset comparison**: side-by-side reports for two or more datasets,
  useful for train/test drift analysis.
- **Scalability**: sampling, minimal mode, and Spark support for datasets
  that do not fit comfortably in memory.
- **Flexible output**: interactive HTML, embeddable widgets for Jupyter, and
  JSON for machine-readable pipelines.

## Compatibility

ydata-profiling supports Python 3.9 and later, and pandas versions from 1.1
up to (but not including) 3.0. For backwards compatibility, the package can
also be imported as `pandas_profiling`:

```python
import ydata_profiling  # preferred
import pandas_profiling  # legacy alias, still works
```

## License

ydata-profiling is released under the MIT license. See the
[changelog](reference/changelog.md) for the release history and the
[history page](reference/history.md) for the story of the project.

# Installation

## From PyPI

The recommended way to install ydata-profiling is from PyPI:

```bash
pip install -U ydata-profiling
```

This pulls in the core dependencies (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy,
visions, pydantic, and others) automatically.

## Optional extras

Several features require additional packages, available as extras:

```bash
pip install "ydata-profiling[notebook]"  # Jupyter widgets support
pip install "ydata-profiling[spark]"     # PySpark DataFrame support
pip install "ydata-profiling[unicode]"   # improved Unicode category plots
pip install "ydata-profiling[test]"      # pytest and coverage tooling
```

## From source

To install the latest development version, clone the repository and install
in editable mode:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling.git
cd ydata-profiling
pip install -e ".[test,notebook]"
```

## Verifying the installation

```bash
python -c "import ydata_profiling; print(ydata_profiling.__version__)"
ydata_profiling --help
```

The package also ships a command-line interface, so after installation the
`ydata_profiling` (and legacy `pandas_profiling`) commands are available on
your PATH.

!!! note
    If you are upgrading from `pandas-profiling` (version 3.x), uninstall it
    first to avoid import conflicts: `pip uninstall pandas-profiling`.

# Quickstart

The fastest way to get a feel for ydata-profiling is to generate your first
report. All it takes is a DataFrame and two lines of code.

## Your first report

```python
import pandas as pd
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": [23, 45, 31, 35, 52, 41],
    "city": ["Lisbon", "Porto", "Lisbon", "Coimbra", "Porto", None],
    "subscribed": [True, False, True, True, False, True],
})

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="My first report")
profile.to_file("report.html")
```

Open `report.html` in a browser and explore the sections: an overview with
dataset-level statistics and alerts, one detailed block per variable, the
correlation matrices, and the missing-values map.

## In a Jupyter notebook

Inside a notebook you can render the report inline instead of writing a file:

```python
profile.to_notebook_iframe()
```

With the `notebook` extra installed, `profile.to_widgets()` renders an
interactive widget version of the report.

## From the command line

For quick one-off profiling, the CLI reads CSV files directly:

```bash
ydata_profiling my_data.csv report.html
ydata_profiling --minimal my_data.csv minimal_report.html
```

## Machine-readable output

When the report feeds another tool rather than a human, export JSON:

```python
profile.to_file("report.json")
```

or get the description as a Python dictionary with
`profile.get_description()` and access individual statistics directly.

args.content:
# Concepts

Understanding a few core concepts makes it much easier to configure
ydata-profiling effectively.

## Type inference with visions

ydata-profiling does not rely on pandas dtypes alone. It uses the
[visions](https://github.com/dylan-profiler/visions) type system to infer the
*semantic* type of each column — a string column may be detected as
categorical, text, a URL, or a file path; an integer column may really be a
boolean or a date. The inferred type determines which statistics are
computed: text columns get character and word distributions, URLs get domain
counts, images get dimension and EXIF summaries.

## The report structure

A report is organised into sections:

- **Overview**: dataset-level statistics (number of variables, rows, missing
  cells, duplicates, memory usage) and data quality alerts.
- **Variables**: one expandable block per column with descriptive statistics,
  a histogram or frequency plot, and type-specific details.
- **Interactions**: scatter plots of pairs of variables (disabled by default
  for wide datasets).
- **Correlations**: heatmaps for the configured correlation metrics.
- **Missing values**: counts, matrix, and (for smaller datasets) dendrogram
  views of missingness.
- **Sample**: the first and last rows of the dataset, and duplicate rows
  when present.

## Configuration model

All behaviour is controlled by a hierarchical settings object
(`ydata_profiling.config.Settings`), loaded from YAML. Settings can be
overridden per report — either with keyword arguments
(`ProfileReport(df, minimal=True)`), by mutating
`profile.config`, or by loading a custom YAML file. See
[changing settings](../advanced_settings/changing_settings.md) for details.

## Descriptions as data

Internally, rendering a report is a two-step process: first the dataset is
*described* into a plain dictionary of statistics, then that description is
*rendered* to HTML, widgets, or JSON. You can hook into the first step with
`profile.get_description()` to build your own tooling on top of the computed
statistics.

# Examples

The repository's `examples/` directory contains runnable scripts covering the
main use cases. Each script loads (or synthesizes) a dataset, builds a
`ProfileReport` with a configuration that highlights a particular feature,
and writes a self-contained HTML report.

## Standard datasets

| Script | Highlights |
| --- | --- |
| `examples/titanic/titanic.py` | Classic mixed-type dataset; the canonical starting point |
| `examples/census/census.py` | US census data; heavy-tailed numerics and categoricals |
| `examples/nza/nza.py` | Dutch accident data with dates and coordinates |

"""Tests for comparing multiple reports."""
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport, compare


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def reports():
    df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": range(20), "b": list("abcdefghij") * 2})
    df2 = pd.DataFrame({"a": range(20, 40), "b": list("klmnopqrst") * 2})
    r1 = ProfileReport(df1, title="Dataset 1", minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
    r2 = ProfileReport(df2, title="Dataset 2", minimal=True, progress_bar=False)
    return r1, r2


class TestCompare:
    def test_compare_html(self, reports):
        comparison = compare(list(reports))
        html = comparison.to_html()
        assert len(html) > 1000
        assert "Dataset 1" in html
        assert "Dataset 2" in html

    def test_compare_json_structure(self, reports):
        comparison = compare(list(reports))
        desc = comparison.get_description()
        assert desc["table"]["n"][0] == 20
        assert desc["table"]["n"][1] == 20
        assert set(desc["variables"]["a"]["mean"].keys()) == {"Dataset 1", "Dataset 2"}

    def test_compare_requires_reports(self):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            compare([])

    def test_compare_rejects_single_report(self, reports):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            compare([reports[0]])

    def test_compare_to_file(self, reports, tmp_path):
        comparison = compare(list(reports))
        out = tmp_path / "comparison.html"
        comparison.to_file(out)
        assert out.exists() and out.stat().st_size > 1000

# Profiling big data

Datasets with millions of rows or hundreds of columns can make a full
profile slow to compute and heavy to render. ydata-profiling offers several
strategies, roughly in order of preference.

## Minimal mode

`minimal=True` disables the most expensive computations — correlations,
interactions, and several detailed per-variable statistics — while keeping
the essentials: types, missing values, duplicates, and descriptive
statistics.

```python
profile = ProfileReport(large_df, minimal=True, title="Large dataset")
```

This is the first thing to try: it is often several times faster than the
default configuration and is usually enough for a first look at a big table.

## Sampling

Instead of computing over the full dataset, profile a representative sample:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, sample={"name": "10% sample", "frac": 0.1})
```

or a fixed number of rows:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, sample={"name": "10k rows", "n": 10000})
```

The report notes the sample size so readers know the statistics are
estimates. Sampling preserves the row order of the underlying draw, so for
time-ordered data prefer shuffling first or use `tsmode`.

## Per-computation tuning

For finer control, disable individual expensive sections:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df)
profile.config.interactions.continuous = False
profile.config.correlations = {}          # skip all correlation matrices
profile.config.missing_diagrams = {}      # skip missing-value diagrams
```

Correlations are quadratic in the number of numeric columns, so dropping
them matters most on wide tables. See
[available settings](../advanced_settings/available_settings.md) for the
full list of knobs.

## Spark

When the data does not fit on one machine at all, profile a Spark DataFrame
directly — ydata-profiling computes the statistics in the Spark cluster.
See the [PySpark integration](../integrations/pyspark.md).

# Comparing datasets

`ydata_profiling.compare` places two or more reports side by side, making it
easy to spot distribution drift between a training and a production
snapshot, before/after a data cleaning step, or any pair of related tables.

## Basic usage

```python
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport, compare

train_report = ProfileReport(train_df, title="Train")
prod_report = ProfileReport(prod_df, title="Production")

comparison = compare([train_report, prod_report])
comparison.to_file("comparison.html")
```

The resulting report shows each statistic and histogram for both datasets
overlaid, so differences in distributions, missingness, and cardinality are
visible at a glance.

## Comparing more than two datasets

Pass any number of reports; labelling each one keeps the output readable:

```python
reports = [
    ProfileReport(df_jan, title="January"),
    ProfileReport(df_feb, title="February"),
    ProfileReport(df_mar, title="March"),
]
compare(reports).to_file("quarterly_drift.html")
```

## Tips

- Use the same configuration for all reports being compared — different
  correlation settings or bin counts make side-by-side plots misleading.
  The simplest approach is to build all reports from one shared config.
- Comparison works on the *description* level, so you can also compare JSON
  exports produced at different times or on different machines.
- For large datasets, profile samples of each dataset with the same random
  seed strategy so the comparison is fair.

See `examples/features/eda_dataset_compare.py` for a runnable demo.

# Custom report appearance

Reports can be restyled without touching the rendering code: titles,
logos, colour themes, and even the inline CSS are configurable.

## Title and metadata

```python
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    title="Quarterly sales — Q1",
    dataset={
        "description": "Aggregated sales from the CRM export.",
        "author": "Data Platform team",
        "url": "https://intranet.example.com/datasets/sales-q1",
    },
)
```

The dataset block is shown in the overview section and is a good place for
provenance information. See [metadata](metadata.md) for the full structure.

## Colour themes

Two built-in themes mimic the Bootswatch palettes:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Flatly theme")
profile.config.html.style.theme = "flatly"   # or "united"
```

A theme changes the accent colours of headers, tables, and plots. Demos are
in `examples/features/theme_flatly_demo.py` and
`examples/features/theme_united_demo.py`.

## Custom styling

For full control, override colours, fonts, and the logo directly:

```python
profile.config.html.style.primary_color = "#0057b8"
profile.config.html.style.logo = "https://example.com/logo.svg"
profile.config.html.style.full_width = True
```

The HTML report is a single self-contained file: all CSS and assets are
inlined, so styled reports can be emailed or hosted anywhere without extra
infrastructure.

## Controlling the layout

- `profile.config.html.navbar_show = False` hides the navigation bar for
  embedding.
- `profile.config.plot.dpi` and `profile.config.plot.image_format`
  (`"svg"` or `"png"`) tune plot crispness versus file size.

# Metadata and dataset descriptions

A profile is far more useful when it records *what* the data is and *where
it came from*. ydata-profiling lets you attach this metadata to the report
instead of keeping it in a separate document nobody reads.

## Dataset metadata

```python
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    title="Customer churn extract",
    dataset={
        "description": "Monthly snapshot of active customers joined with churn labels.",
        "creator": "Analytics Engineering",
        "author": "J. Doe",
        "copyright_holder": "Example Corp",
        "copyright_year": "2026",
        "url": "https://data.example.com/catalog/churn",
    },
)
```

All fields are optional; provided ones are rendered in the overview section
and included in JSON exports, so downstream tooling can pick them up.

## Column descriptions

Human-readable explanations per column live under
`variables.descriptions`:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Annotated report")
profile.config.variables.descriptions = {
    "tenure_months": "Number of months the customer has been active.",
    "churn": "1 if the customer cancelled within the period.",
}
```

Descriptions appear next to the variable statistics — especially valuable
for cryptic column names inherited from source systems.

## Why bother?

Profiling reports tend to outlive the analysis that produced them: they get
attached to tickets, linked from data catalogues, and rediscovered months
later. Embedding provenance and semantics in the report itself means the
context travels with the statistics, and the JSON export doubles as a
machine-readable data dictionary.

# Handling sensitive data

Reports often get shared more widely than the raw data. A single HTML file
containing names, identifiers, or rare value combinations can leak more
than intended, so ydata-profiling provides a *sensitive mode*.

## Sensitive mode

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="HR extract (anonymized)", sensitive=True)
```

With `sensitive=True`:

- the **Samples** section (head, tail, and duplicate rows) is omitted, so
  no raw records appear in the report;
- category-level detail for categorical and text columns is reduced.

Statistics such as counts, means, and histograms are still computed — the
report remains useful for understanding distributions without exposing
individual records.

## What sensitive mode is *not*

Sensitive mode reduces disclosure risk; it is not anonymization. Aggregate
statistics can still reveal information about small groups (e.g. a category
with a single member). Before sharing a report on genuinely confidential
data:

1. Drop or hash direct identifiers (emails, national IDs) from the DataFrame
   *before* profiling.
2. Review high-cardinality columns — unique values are listed in frequency
   tables.
3. Consider reporting on a sample so exact counts are not recoverable.

## Combining with other settings

Sensitive mode composes with the rest of the configuration. A common
pattern is a shareable "external" report and a full internal one:

```python
external = ProfileReport(df, title="External", sensitive=True, minimal=True)
internal = ProfileReport(df, title="Internal")
```

See `examples/features/mask_sensitive.py` for a runnable example.

# Time series datasets

Standard profiling assumes rows are exchangeable. For time series that
assumption is wrong — order matters — so ydata-profiling has a dedicated
time series mode.

## Enabling time series mode

```python
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    tsmode=True,
    sortby="timestamp",
    title="Air quality over time",
)
```

Two things change in `tsmode`:

- **Line plots replace histograms** for the overview of numeric variables,
  showing each series against row order (or the sorted timestamp) so trends,
  seasonality, and regime shifts are visible.
- **Autocorrelation plots** (ACF/PACF) are added per numeric variable, which
  help spot lag structure before modelling.

`sortby` accepts a column name or a list of columns; sort before profiling
if the DataFrame index order is not chronological.

## Choosing variables

Not every column benefits from the time series treatment. Identifier-like
columns are better left alone:

```python
profile.config.vars.num.low_categorical_threshold = 5
profile.config.timeseries.active = True
```

The `timeseries` settings group controls which variables get the line-plot
and autocorrelation treatment.

## Practical notes

- Keep the series contiguous where possible; large gaps make the line plots
  misleading. Resampling to a regular frequency first often produces a
  clearer report.
- For very long series, combine `tsmode` with a
  [sample](big_data.md#sampling) taken as a contiguous window rather than a
  random fraction, so the ordering information is preserved.
- A runnable example is `examples/usaairquality/usaairquality.py`.

"""Tests for duplicates detection and the Discretizer."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from ydata_profiling.config import Settings
from ydata_profiling.model.duplicates import get_duplicates
from ydata_profiling.model.pandas.discretize_pandas import (
    DiscretizationType,
    Discretizer,
)


class TestGetDuplicates:
    def test_known_duplicates(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 2, 1], "b": [3, 4, 4, 3]})
        config = Settings()
        metrics, duplicates = get_duplicates(config, df, list(df.columns))
        assert metrics["n_duplicates"] == 2
        assert metrics["p_duplicates"] == 0.5
        assert len(duplicates) == 2

    def test_no_duplicates(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
        config = Settings()
        metrics, duplicates = get_duplicates(config, df, list(df.columns))
        assert metrics["n_duplicates"] == 0
        assert metrics["p_duplicates"] == 0.0

    def test_missing_duplicates_key(self):
        df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
        config = Settings()
        # Only a subset of columns supported -> no duplicate detection
        metrics, duplicates = get_duplicates(config, df, [])
        assert metrics == {}
        assert duplicates is None


class TestDiscretizer:

        config = Settings()
        # Only a subset of columns supported -> no duplicate detection
        metrics, duplicates = get_duplicates(config, df, [])

# Available settings

All report behaviour is driven by a hierarchical settings tree, defined in
`ydata_profiling.config.Settings` (a pydantic model, so unknown keys and
wrong types fail loudly). This page maps out the main branches; the
defaults live in
`src/ydata_profiling/config_default.yaml` in the repository.

## Top-level options

| Setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `"Pandas Profiling Report"` | Report title shown in the header |
| `minimal` | `False` | Cheapest useful profile: no correlations, interactions, or detailed plots |
| `sensitive` | `False` | Omit samples and category detail (see [sensitive data](../features/sensitive_data.md)) |
| `tsmode` | `False` | Time series mode: line plots and autocorrelation |
| `explorative` | `False` | Opposite of minimal: enables everything, including interactions |
| `sample` | `None` | Dict like `{"name": ..., "n": ...}` or `{"frac": ...}` to profile a sample |
| `sortby` | `None` | Column(s) to sort by before profiling |
| `dark_mode` / `orange_mode` | `False` | Built-in colour schemes |

## Branch highlights

- **`vars.num` / `vars.cat` / `vars.text`** — bin counts, quantile lists,
  low-categorical thresholds, and per-type toggles.
- **`correlations`** — one sub-setting per metric: `pearson`, `spearman`,
  `kendall`, `cramers`, `phi_k`, plus `auto` which picks per column type.
  Each has `calculate` and a `threshold`/`warn` level used for alerts.
- **`interactions`** — `continuous` toggles pairwise scatter plots (off by
  default; quadratic cost).
- **`missing_diagrams`** — `matrix`, `bar`, `heatmap`, `dendrogram` toggles.
- **`plot`** — DPI, image format (`png`/`svg`), histogram binning, and
  correlation plot arguments.
- **`html.style`** — `theme`, `primary_color`, `logo`, `full_width`; see
  [custom reports](../features/custom_reports.md).
- **`duplicates` / `samples`** — how many duplicate rows and head/tail rows
  to include.
- **`dataset` / `variables.descriptions`** — metadata covered in
  [metadata](../features/metadata.md).
- **`n_obs_unique` / `n_freq_table_max`** — caps that keep rendering
  tractable on high-cardinality data.
- **`progress_bar`, `pool_size`** — UI and parallelism controls.

## Inspecting the effective configuration

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df)
print(profile.config.json(indent=2))  # the full resolved settings tree
```

Because settings are a pydantic model, `config.json()` is a reliable way to
see exactly what a report used — handy when filing bug reports.

# Changing settings

There are four ways to change the configuration, from most common to most
powerful. They can be combined; later overrides win.

## 1. Constructor shorthands

The most common options are keyword arguments on `ProfileReport`:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    title="Sales data",
    minimal=True,
    explorative=False,
    sensitive=False,
    dark_mode=False,
    sample={"name": "10k sample", "n": 10000},
)
```

## 2. Mutating `profile.config`

Anything in the settings tree can be changed through attribute assignment.
Because the tree is validated by pydantic, typos raise immediately:

```python
profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Customised")
profile.config.vars.num.n_quantiles = 100
profile.config.plot.histogram.bins = 50
profile.config.correlations["spearman"].calculate = False
profile.config.html.style.primary_color = "#2a9d8f"
```

## 3. YAML configuration files

For reproducible, shareable setups, keep settings in a YAML file:

```yaml
# config_minimal.yaml
title: "Warehouse snapshot"
minimal: true
plot:
  dpi: 150
  image_format: svg
correlations:
  kendall:
    calculate: false
```

```python
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, config_file="config_minimal.yaml")
```

The file is merged over the defaults, so you only specify what changes.

## 4. Loading and dumping `Settings` directly

```python
from ydata_profiling.config import Settings

settings = Settings()
settings.minimal = True
profile = ProfileReport(df, config=settings)

# Round-trip through JSON for storage:
restored = Settings.parse_raw(settings.json())
```

## Recommendations

- Put shared organisation-wide defaults in a committed YAML file and pass it
  via `config_file`; keep one-off tweaks as constructor arguments.
- When reporting a bug, attach `profile.config.json()` output so
  maintainers can reproduce the exact configuration.

args.content:
# Caching

Profiling recomputes statistics every time a report is built. During an
iterative session — tweaking settings, re-rendering, comparing outputs —
this gets slow. ydata-profiling caches intermediate results on disk so
repeated runs only redo what changed.

## How it works

Expensive computations (per-variable descriptions, correlation matrices)
are memoized through [joblib](https://joblib.readthedocs.io/)'s `Memory`.
The cache key covers the input data and the relevant settings, so changing
a setting invalidates only the parts that depend on it.

## Choosing the cache location

By default a temporary directory is used. Point it somewhere persistent to
share the cache across processes and reboots:

```python
from joblib import Memory
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Cached run")
profile.config.vars.low_categorical_threshold = 0  # example tweak
```

Set the cache directory via the `YDATA_PROFILING_CACHE_DIR`-style
environment/joblib configuration, or construct a `Memory` instance and use
it when building your own pipelines around `get_description()`.

## When caching helps — and when it does not

- **Helps**: repeated reports over the same DataFrame while iterating on
  settings; CI jobs that regenerate the same reports.
- **Does not help**: one-off reports; data that changes every run (the
  cache key includes the data, so new data means a cold cache).

## Housekeeping

The cache is not size-managed automatically. If you use a persistent
directory, clear it periodically:

```python
memory = Memory(".cache/ydata_profiling", verbose=0)
memory.clear()
```

Keep the cache directory out of version control — add it to `.gitignore`.

# Analytics and telemetry

ydata-profiling can emit anonymous usage events that help the maintainers
understand which features are used and where the library is slow or
fragile. This page explains what is collected and how to opt out.

## What is collected

Events are coarse-grained and contain **no data**: things like "a report was
generated with N rows and M columns", which optional features were enabled
(`tsmode`, `sensitive`, `minimal`), how long rendering took, and the
library/Python versions. Column names, values, and report contents are
never included.

## Opting out

Telemetry is off unless explicitly enabled. If your environment has it on
(for example via an organisation-wide configuration), disable it by setting
the environment variable before importing:

```bash
export YDATA_PROFILING_NO_ANALYTICS=true
```

or programmatically:

```python
import os
os.environ["YDATA_PROFILING_NO_ANALYTICS"] = "true"

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport  # import after setting the flag
```

When analytics are disabled, no network calls are made during profiling.

## Checking your environment

In locked-down environments (no outbound network), analytics silently
no-op; report generation does not depend on them. If you see unexpected
network traffic, verify the flag above is set in the environment of the
process actually running Python — notebook kernels and schedulers often
have their own environment.

## Questions

The implementation lives in `ydata_profiling/utils/tracking.py` in the
source tree and is the authoritative reference for exactly which events
exist. Concerns can be raised via a GitHub issue.

# Caching

This page covers the two kinds of caching relevant to ydata-profiling:
the built-in dataset download cache, and caching *you* add around report
generation for repeated runs.

## Built-in dataset cache

The helper functions used by the example scripts and tutorials
(`ydata_profiling.utils.cache.cache_file` and `cache_zipped_file`) download
a dataset over HTTP once and store it in a local data directory. On
subsequent calls the cached file is reused instead of downloading again:

```python
from ydata_profiling.utils.cache import cache_file

path = cache_file("titanic.csv", "https://example.org/titanic.csv")
```

The cache location is resolved by `ydata_profiling.utils.paths.get_data_path()`
— a `data/` directory in the current working context. Delete that directory
to force re-downloads, and keep it out of version control.

Note that the profiling computation itself (descriptive statistics,
correlations, plots) is **not** memoized by the library: every
`ProfileReport(...)` call recomputes from the DataFrame it is given.

## Caching report outputs yourself

When you regenerate the same report repeatedly — nightly jobs, CI, notebook
re-runs — cache at the *artifact* level instead:

- **HTML/JSON exports**: store `profile.to_file(...)` output keyed by a hash
  of the input data and the configuration (`profile.config.json()` is a
  stable serialization of the settings). If the key matches, skip the
  computation entirely.
- **Descriptions**: `profile.get_description()` returns a plain dictionary
  that is cheap to pickle and reload:

```python
import hashlib
import pickle

import pandas as pd
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

def cached_description(df: pd.DataFrame, cache_dir=".cache/profiling"):
    key = hashlib.sha256(pd.util.hash_pandas_object(df).values).hexdigest()
    path = f"{cache_dir}/{key}.pkl"
    try:
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            return pickle.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        import os
        os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
        desc = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True).get_description()
        with open(path, "wb") as f:
            pickle.dump(desc, f)
        return desc
```

## Practical notes

- Include the library version in the cache key — statistics and schema can
  change between releases, making stale caches misleading.
- For [dataset comparison](../features/comparing_datasets.md), caching the
  per-dataset descriptions lets you compare a new snapshot against many
  historical ones without recomputing them.

# Analytics and usage data

This page summarizes what the library does (and does not do) with respect
to analytics and outbound network calls, and how to keep report generation
fully offline.

## What ydata-profiling sends

The core profiling pipeline — describing a DataFrame and rendering a
report — makes **no network calls**. Statistics are computed locally from
the DataFrame you pass in, and the HTML report inlines all of its assets
(CSS, JavaScript, images as base64), so viewing a report does not phone
home either.

Network access only happens when your own code triggers it, typically:

- downloading example datasets with
  `ydata_profiling.utils.cache.cache_file` / `cache_zipped_file`;
- loading data yourself with `pandas.read_csv("https://...")`-style URLs.

## Keeping it fully offline

For air-gapped or compliance-sensitive environments:

1. Provide data locally (files, databases) rather than via URLs.
2. Ship fonts and viewer assets with the report — the default self-contained
   HTML already does this, so no extra step is needed.
3. If you distribute reports externally, review them before sharing:
   frequency tables and sample rows can contain identifying values. See
   [sensitive data](../features/sensitive_data.md) for the built-in
   `sensitive=True` mode.

## Verifying locally

You can confirm the offline behaviour empirically: generate a report inside
a network namespace without connectivity, or simply run with networking
disabled for the process — report generation succeeds either way, because
nothing in the render path requires it.

## Questions

If you observe unexpected network activity during profiling, please open an
issue with the ydata-profiling version, your configuration
(`profile.config.json()`), and a description of the traffic so the
maintainers can investigate.

# PySpark integration

For datasets that live in a Spark cluster, ydata-profiling can profile a
Spark DataFrame directly — statistics are computed with Spark operations,
so the data never needs to fit in the driver's memory.

## Installation

```bash
pip install "ydata-profiling[spark]"
```

This installs `pyspark` and `pyarrow`. A working Java runtime is required
for local Spark sessions.

## Usage

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[*]").getOrCreate()
sdf = spark.read.parquet("s3://bucket/events/")

profile = ProfileReport(sdf, title="Events (Spark)")
profile.to_file("events_report.html")
```

`ProfileReport` detects the Spark DataFrame type and dispatches to the
Spark backend automatically — the API is identical to the pandas case, and
so is the resulting report.

## Notes and limitations

- Spark profiling computes most of the same statistics as the pandas
  backend, but a few pandas-specific details (certain interactions and
  diagram types) may differ or be unavailable. Check the alerts section of
  the generated report for anything that was skipped.
- Sampling still helps: `sample={"frac": 0.1}` translates into a Spark
  `sample`, reducing shuffle and compute time on very large tables.
- Cache (`sdf.cache()`) a DataFrame before profiling if it is the result of
  a long lineage — profiling triggers multiple passes over the data.
- A runnable example is `examples/features/spark_example.py`.

# Great Expectations integration

ydata-profiling answers "what does my data look like?"; Great Expectations
answers "does my data satisfy the rules I care about?". The two compose
naturally: profile first to understand the data, then turn what you learn
into expectations.

## Generating an expectation suite from a profile

The integration builds a Great Expectations suite from the statistics a
report already computed:

```python
import great_expectations as gx
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Orders", minimal=True, explorative=False)

suite = profile.to_expectation_suite(
    suite_name="orders_suite",
    data_context_type="ephemeral",
    run_validation=True,
    build_suite=True,
)
```

The generated suite encodes expectations derived from the observed data:
column existence and types, null fractions, value ranges for numeric
columns, and sets of observed categories for low-cardinality columns.

## Prerequisites

The integration requires `great_expectations` (install it separately; it is
not a core dependency) and pandas. Save the suite with a real
`DataContext` when you want it to persist:

```python
context = gx.get_context()
context.add_or_update_expectation_suite(expectation_suite=suite)
```

## Typical workflow

1. **Profile** a trusted snapshot (e.g. last month's data) to learn ranges,
   categories, and nullability.
2. **Generate** the expectation suite from that profile.
3. **Hand-tune** the suite — generated expectations describe what *was*,
   not necessarily what *should be*; tighten bounds based on domain
   knowledge.
4. **Validate** new batches against the suite in your pipeline, and
   re-profile periodically to detect drift the expectations do not cover.

# IDE integrations

ydata-profiling works in any Python environment, but a few integrations
make the loop tighter in the tools people actually use.

## Jupyter and JupyterLab

The first-class environment. Render reports inline:

```python
profile.to_notebook_iframe()   # iframe-embedded HTML
profile.to_widgets()           # interactive ipywidgets version
```

`to_widgets()` requires the `notebook` extra
(`pip install "ydata-profiling[notebook]"`) and ipywidgets enabled in the
frontend. The iframe variant works everywhere HTML output is supported,
including JupyterLab, VS Code notebooks, and Google Colab.

## VS Code

In VS Code notebooks, `to_notebook_iframe()` renders in the cell output.
For standalone scripts, write the report to a file and open it with the
built-in preview or Live Preview extension:

```python
profile.to_file("report.html")
```

The repository ships a `.devcontainer` with the Python extension, black,
and pytest preconfigured — open the folder in a container to get a
ready-made development environment.

## PyCharm

PyCharm's Scientific mode displays DataFrames and supports notebook cells,
where the iframe output works as in Jupyter. For script runs, generate the
HTML file and use *Open in Browser*. Set the matplotlib backend to `Agg`
in headless run configurations to avoid GUI backend issues.

## Other editors

Any editor works: the report is a plain HTML file. A small helper keeps the
flow fast:

```python
import webbrowser
profile.to_file("report.html")
webbrowser.open("report.html")
```

# Pipeline integrations

Profiling fits naturally into data pipelines as a data-quality gate or an
observability artifact. The library is orchestrator-agnostic — it is just a
Python call — but a few patterns work well across Airflow, Dagster,
Prefect, Luigi, and plain cron.

## Pattern: profile as a task artifact

Generate a report for every materialized table and store the HTML as a task
artifact (S3, GCS, or the orchestrator's artifact store):

```python
def profile_task(df, output_uri, run_id):
    profile = ProfileReport(
        df,
        title=f"orders @ {run_id}",
        minimal=True,  # keep runtime predictable in pipelines
    )
    profile.to_file(output_uri)
```

Minimal mode keeps runtime and memory bounded, which matters when the task
shares a worker with other jobs.

## Pattern: JSON export for machine checks

When the pipeline should *react* to the data, export JSON and assert on
statistics instead of eyeballing HTML:

```python
desc = ProfileReport(df, minimal=True).get_description()
table = desc["table"]

assert table["n_cells_missing"] == 0, "unexpected missing values"
assert table["n_duplicates"] / table["n"] < 0.01, "duplicate spike"
```

For declarative checks on top of this, see the
[Great Expectations integration](great_expectations.md).

## Pattern: drift monitoring with compare

Keep the previous period's report description and
[compare](../features/comparing_datasets.md) the new batch against it;
large divergences in distributions are an early warning for upstream
schema or feed changes.

## Operational tips

- Set `progress_bar=False` so logs stay clean.
- Profile a deterministic [sample](../features/big_data.md#sampling) for
  very large tables; document the sample in the report title.
- Treat the library version as part of the pipeline contract: pin it, since
  statistics and report schema can evolve between releases.

# Changelog

All notable changes to ydata-profiling are documented here. The format
follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.0.0/) and the
project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/). Releases are
produced by semantic-release from
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/).

The authoritative, per-release list of changes is on the
[GitHub releases page](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/releases).

## [4.16.1]

### Fixed

- Compatibility fixes for recent numpy and pandas releases.
- Minor report rendering corrections.

## [4.16.0]

### Added

- Continued improvements to the Spark backend and time series mode.

## Migrating from pandas-profiling

If you are coming from `pandas-profiling` 3.x, the breaking changes are
concentrated in the 4.0 release:

- Package renamed to `ydata-profiling` (`import ydata_profiling`; the
  legacy `import pandas_profiling` alias is still provided).
- Configuration system rewritten on top of pydantic — most setting keys are
  unchanged, but validation is stricter.
- `df.profile_report()` remains available as a pandas accessor.

See the [history page](history.md) for the full story of the rename.

args.content:
# History

## Origins

The project started in 2016 as **pandas-profiling**, created by Jos Polfliet
and subsequently maintained by Simon Brugman. The idea was simple: the
`df.describe()` one-liner was useful but far too shallow, and every data
scientist was rewriting the same exploratory boilerplate. pandas-profiling
turned that boilerplate into a single call producing a rich HTML report.

Over the following years the project grew to millions of downloads and
became a default step in exploratory data analysis, adding correlation
metrics (including Phik), missing-value diagrams, dataset comparison, and
configurable report styling.

## The move to YData

In 2022 the project joined [YData](https://ydata.ai) and was renamed
**ydata-profiling**, starting with version 4.0. The rename came with a
modernized codebase:

- configuration rebuilt on pydantic models with strict validation;
- a pluggable backend architecture, enabling support beyond pandas —
  notably Apache Spark DataFrames;
- time series mode (`tsmode`) with line plots and autocorrelation;
- continued compatibility via the `pandas_profiling` import alias and CLI.

## Today

ydata-profiling remains MIT-licensed open source, developed in the open at
[github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling).
It is maintained by YData together with community contributors — see the
[contribution guidelines](../support-contribution/contribution_guidelines.md)
if you would like to get involved, and [resources](resources.md) for talks,
articles, and related projects.

# Resources

Pointers to material that helps you get more out of ydata-profiling.

## Code and community

- **Source code and issue tracker**:
  [github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling)
- **PyPI package**: [pypi.org/project/ydata-profiling](https://pypi.org/project/ydata-profiling/)
- **Discord community**: [discord.ydata.ai](https://discord.ydata.ai) —
  the fastest way to get usage questions answered.

## Examples

The [examples directory](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/tree/develop/examples)
in the repository contains runnable scripts for every major feature:
standard datasets (Titanic, census, meteorites), dataset comparison,
sensitive-data masking, theming, Spark, image and URL types, and time
series profiling. The [examples page](../getting-started/examples.md) lists
them with a one-line description each.

## Related projects in the ecosystem

- **YData Fabric / synthetic data**: generate privacy-preserving synthetic
  data informed by profiling statistics.
- **visions**: the semantic type system ydata-profiling uses for type
  inference ([github.com/dylan-profiler/visions](https://github.com/dylan-profiler/visions)).
- **phik**: the φk correlation library used for mixed-type correlation
  matrices.
- **Great Expectations**: data validation that pairs well with profiling —
  see the [integration guide](../integrations/great_expectations.md).

## Citing

If ydata-profiling contributes to academic work, please cite the repository
and the version used. Including `ydata_profiling.__version__` in your
methods section makes analyses reproducible.

# Common issues

A curated list of the problems users hit most often, with fixes.

## Report generation is very slow

- Wide datasets: correlations are quadratic in the number of numeric
  columns. Use `minimal=True`, or disable specific matrices via
  `profile.config.correlations`.
- Long datasets: profile a [sample](../features/big_data.md#sampling).
- High-cardinality text columns: frequency tables and word clouds are
  expensive; cap them via `n_freq_table_max` and text settings.

## `MemoryError` or the kernel dies

Rendering keeps the full report (including base64-encoded plots) in memory.
Use `minimal=True`, reduce plot DPI (`config.plot.dpi`), switch plots to
PNG instead of SVG (`config.plot.image_format = "png"`), and sample the
data. For truly large data, use the [Spark backend](../integrations/pyspark.md).

## Widgets do not render in Jupyter

`to_widgets()` needs the `notebook` extra and a working ipywidgets
frontend. If widgets fail or you are on Colab/VS Code, use
`to_notebook_iframe()` instead — it has no widget dependency.

## Column inferred with the wrong type

Type inference is heuristic. Force the type with a custom typeset (see
`examples/type_schema.py`) or recode the column before profiling. Dates
stored as strings are the most common case — parse them with
`pd.to_datetime` first.

## Conda/pip dependency conflicts

ydata-profiling pins upper bounds on several scientific libraries. Create a
fresh virtual environment rather than installing into a heavily populated
one, and upgrade `pip` first so it can resolve wheels properly.

## `UnicodeDecodeError` reading input files

The CLI assumes UTF-8. Convert the file (`iconv`) or load it in pandas with
an explicit `encoding=` argument and profile the DataFrame from Python.

## Spark errors

Spark support requires the `spark` extra and a Java runtime. `JAVA_HOME`
unset or an unsupported Java version is the usual cause of opaque
`pyspark` startup failures.

- Long datasets: profile a [sample](../features/big_data.md#sampling).
- High-cardinality text columns: frequency tables and word clouds are
  expensive; cap them via `n_freq_table_max` and text settings.

## `MemoryError` or the kernel dies

Rendering keeps the full report (including base64-encoded plots) in memory.
Use `minimal=True`, reduce plot DPI (`config.plot.dpi`), switch plots to
PNG instead of SVG (`config.plot.image_format = "png"`), and sample the
data. For truly large data, use the [Spark backend](../integrations/pyspark.md).

## Widgets do not render in Jupyter

`to_widgets()` needs the `notebook` extra and a working ipywidgets
frontend. If widgets fail or you are on Colab/VS Code, use
`to_notebook_iframe()` instead — it has no widget dependency.

## Column inferred with the wrong type

Type inference is heuristic. Force the type with a custom typeset (see
`examples/type_schema.py`) or recode the column before profiling. Dates
stored as strings are the most common case — parse them with
`pd.to_datetime` first.

## Conda/pip dependency conflicts

ydata-profiling pins upper bounds on several scientific libraries. Create a
fresh virtual environment rather than installing into a heavily populated
one, and upgrade `pip` first so it can resolve wheels properly.

## `UnicodeDecodeError` reading input files

The CLI assumes UTF-8. Convert the file (`iconv`) or load it in pandas with
an explicit `encoding=` argument and profile the DataFrame from Python.

## Spark errors

Spark support requires the `spark` extra and a Java runtime. `JAVA_HOME`
unset or an unsupported Java version is the usual cause of opaque
`pyspark` startup failures.

# Contribution guidelines

This page expands on the `CONTRIBUTING.md` file at the repository root.

## Setting up a development environment

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling.git
cd ydata-profiling
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
make install-dev   # editable install + test/lint tooling + pre-commit
```

Alternatively, open the repository in the provided
[devcontainer](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/tree/develop/.devcontainer)
for a fully provisioned environment.

## Running tests and checks

```bash
make test    # pytest over tests/
make lint    # black --check + isort --check
make format  # apply both formatters
```

Tests that need optional dependencies (pyspark, ipywidgets,
great_expectations) skip automatically when those are not installed.

## Branching and commits

- Development happens on `develop`; releases are cut to `master` by
  semantic-release.
- Branch names: `feat/<slug>`, `fix/<slug>`, `docs/<slug>`.
- Commits must follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
  (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`, ...).
  commitlint and the Semantic Pull Request app enforce this on PR titles.

## Pull request expectations

- One logical change per PR; fill in the PR template completely.
- New behavior needs tests; bug fixes should include a regression test that
  fails without the fix.
- Update the docs (`docs/`) when user-facing behavior changes.
- Keep diffs minimal — drive-by refactors make reviews slower.

## Documentation contributions

Docs are built with MkDocs Material. Run `make docs-serve` for a live
preview on <http://127.0.0.1:8000> while editing pages under `docs/`.

# Help & troubleshooting

Where to get help, and how to ask for it effectively.

## Before you ask

1. Check the [common issues](common_issues.md) page — most performance and
   environment problems are covered there.
2. Search [existing GitHub issues](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/issues);
   many questions have already been answered.
3. Upgrade to the latest release (`pip install -U ydata-profiling`) and
   confirm the problem persists.

## Getting a useful answer fast

Whether on GitHub or Discord, a good report contains:

- **Version information**: `ydata_profiling.__version__`, pandas, numpy,
  Python version, and OS.
- **The configuration used**: `print(profile.config.json())` — many
  "bugs" are configuration surprises.
- **A minimal reproducible example**: the smallest code snippet (ideally
  with synthetic data generated by numpy/pandas) that shows the problem.
  Never post confidential data.
- **The full traceback** or a screenshot of the unexpected output.

## Channels

- **Bug reports**: use the
  [bug report form](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/issues/new?template=bug_report_form.yaml).
- **Feature requests**: use the
  [feature request form](https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling/issues/new?template=feature_request_form.yaml).
- **Usage questions and discussion**: the
  [Discord community](https://discord.ydata.ai) is the fastest channel.
- **Security issues**: do not open public issues; email
  opensource@ydata.ai.

## Debugging on your own

- Run with a tiny DataFrame first: if 100 rows work and 1 million do not,
  it is a scale issue — see [big data](../features/big_data.md).
- `minimal=True` is a quick bisect: if the minimal report works, re-enable
  sections one at a time to find the expensive or failing computation.
- For rendering problems, export JSON (`profile.to_file("report.json")`):
  if JSON works, the description step is fine and the issue is in HTML
  rendering.

"""Titanic dataset example.

Original data source: https://www.openml.org/d/40945 (Titanic survival data).
To keep this example self-contained and offline-friendly, a small synthetic
dataset with the same schema and roughly similar distributions is generated
instead of downloading the file.
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport


def load_titanic(n: int = 891, seed: int = 42) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pclass = rng.choice([1, 2, 3], size=n, p=[0.24, 0.21, 0.55])
    sex = rng.choice(["male", "female"], size=n, p=[0.65, 0.35])
    age = rng.normal(29.0, 14.0, size=n).clip(0.5, 80).round(1)
    # Introduce missing ages, as in the real dataset.
    age[rng.random(n) < 0.2] = np.nan
    fare = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=16.0, size=n).round(2)
    embarked = rng.choice(["S", "C", "Q"], size=n, p=[0.72, 0.19, 0.09])
    # Survival depends weakly on class and sex, mimicking the real pattern.
    p_surv = 0.2 + 0.15 * (pclass == 1) + 0.3 * (sex == "female")
    survived = rng.random(n) < p_surv

    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "pclass": pclass,
            "sex": sex,
            "age": age,
            "sibsp": rng.poisson(0.5, size=n),
            "parch": rng.poisson(0.4, size=n),
            "fare": fare,
            "embarked": embarked,
            "survived": survived.astype(int),
        }
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    df = load_titanic()
    profile = ProfileReport(
        df,
        title="Titanic Dataset",
        dataset={
            "description": "Synthetic stand-in for the Titanic dataset "
            "(original: https://www.openml.org/d/40945)",
        },
    )
    profile.to_file("titanic_report.html")

"""Meteorites dataset example.

Original data source: NASA's Meteoritical Society dataset
https://data.nasa.gov/Space-Science/Meteorite-Landings/gh4g-9sfh
A synthetic dataset with the same columns is generated here so the example
runs offline. Minimal mode is used, as recommended for larger files.
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport


def load_meteorites(n: int = 20000, seed: int = 7) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    classes = ["L5", "L6", "H5", "H4", "H6", "LL6", "CM2", "Iron", "Eucrite"]
    years = rng.integers(1800, 2013, size=n)
    # Mass in grams, heavily right-skewed like the real data.
    mass = rng.lognormal(mean=7.0, sigma=2.5, size=n).round(1)

    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "name": [f"meteorite_{i}" for i in range(n)],
            "id": np.arange(10000, 10000 + n),
            "nametype": "Valid",
            "recclass": rng.choice(classes, size=n),
            "mass": mass,
            "fall": rng.choice(["Fell", "Found"], size=n, p=[0.03, 0.97]),
            "year": pd.to_datetime(years, format="%Y"),
            "reclat": rng.uniform(-90, 90, size=n).round(5),
            "reclong": rng.uniform(-180, 180, size=n).round(5),
        }
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    df = load_meteorites()
    profile = ProfileReport(
        df,
        minimal=True,
        title="Meteorite Landings (synthetic, NASA schema)",
    )
    profile.to_file("meteorites_report.html")

"""NZA (Dutch Surgical Aneurysm Audit) example.

Original data source: https://github.com/ydataai/ydata-profiling example data
(Dutch national aneurysm audit extract).
A synthetic dataset with a similar structure is generated so the example
runs offline. Highlights date columns and categorical medical coding.
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

    return pd.DataFrame(

            "age": rng.normal(41, 11, size=n).clip(18, 95).round().astype(int),
            "job": rng.choice(

                 "services", "retired", "self-employed", "student", "unemployed"],
                size=n,
            ),
            "marital": rng.choice(
                ["married", "single", "divorced"], size=n, p=[0.6, 0.28, 0.12]
            ),
            "education": rng.choice(
                ["primary", "secondary", "tertiary", "unknown"],
                size=n,
                p=[0.15, 0.51, 0.29, 0.05],
            ),
            "default": rng.choice(["no", "yes"], size=n, p=[0.98, 0.02]),
            "balance": rng.normal(1400, 3000, size=n).round().astype(int),
            "housing": rng.choice(["yes", "no"], size=n, p=[0.55, 0.45]),
            "loan": rng.choice(["no", "yes"], size=n, p=[0.84, 0.16]),
            "contact": rng.choice(
                ["cellular", "telephone", "unknown"], size=n, p=[0.65, 0.1, 0.25]
            ),

                size=n,

            "campaign": rng.poisson(2, size=n) + 1,

            "previous": rng.poisson(0.6, size=n),
            "y": rng.choice(["no", "yes"], size=n, p=[0.88, 0.12]),
        }
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":

        df,

    profile.config.vars.num.low_categorical_threshold = 0
    profile.to_file("banking_report.html")
